contributions: a structural (MDP-based) diagnosis that sequence-level efficiency rewards used by prior efficiency-oriented RL methods create an inherent, unavoidable training conflict by penalizing correct-but-long reasoning, since only the first (mode-selection) token actually determines efficiency while all later tokens can only affect correctness

ADaPT, a token-level dual-process framework applying an efficiency-related mode reward exclusively to the <think>/<answer> mode-selection token, decoupling efficiency optimization from correctness optimization at every other position

a CISPO-based first-token-specific ratio-clipping fix, motivated by directly observed evidence that standard PPO/GRPO clipping nullifies the policy gradient at the mode-selection token far more severely than elsewhere, plus a balanced dual-start rollout strategy preventing mode collapse

demonstrated continuous, post-hoc control over the efficiency-performance trade-off (adjusting the <think>-token decoding threshold with no retraining) that traces a genuine Pareto frontier dominating all compared baselines, while preserving the model's full deep-reasoning capability when slow mode is invoked
limitations: The paper does not discuss limitations explicitly in the excerpted sections; ADaPT's two reasoning modes (<think> full-CoT vs. <answer> short/direct) are a binary discretization rather than a continuum, so within-mode length is not separately controlled by the token-level mechanism (the Pareto-frontier control operates by adjusting how often slow mode is triggered, not by continuously varying the length of a slow-mode trace itself). The dual-start balanced-rollout strategy and CISPO first-token stabilization add training-pipeline complexity (a two-stage SFT-then-GRPO procedure with a specialized clipping rule) relative to a single-stage correctness-only RL baseline.
method: Identifies the root cause as sequence-level coupling between efficiency and correctness signals, and derives (via a structural MDP analysis) that efficiency is fully determined by the very first action -- the reasoning-mode choice, i.e. whether the response begins with <think> (slow, full-CoT) or <answer> (fast, direct/short) -- while every subsequent token can only affect correctness, not efficiency, since the mode is already fixed. This implies the reward should be decomposed accordingly rather than applied uniformly across all tokens. ADaPT trains in two stages: (1) SFT cold-start on data annotated with either <think> (long CoT, from an existing long-CoT dataset) or <answer> (short rationale/direct answer) formats, familiarizing the model with both fast and slow reasoning behaviors and their output formats; (2) ADaPT-GRPO, which introduces a token-level mode reward r_think applied only at the very first token (whether <think> was emitted), combining an absolute-quality-threshold term (fast mode is only encouraged when its accuracy Acc_a exceeds a threshold gamma; otherwise <think> is encouraged) and a relative-advantage term (slow mode is encouraged more strongly when it shows clear accuracy gains over fast mode), balanced by weight alpha -- while all subsequent tokens continue to receive only standard sequence-level correctness reward, decoupling mode selection from answer-quality optimization entirely. Because standard PPO/GRPO importance-ratio clipping severely degrades learning specifically at this critical first token (due to a fixed dual-start behavior policy causing much higher empirical clipping rates there than at other positions, observed directly via clipping-ratio tracking during training), a CISPO ratio constraint is applied exclusively to the first token to stabilize its gradient, while all other tokens use the standard GRPO/PPO clipped objective. A balanced dual-start rollout strategy (each training batch split evenly between rollouts forced to start with <think> vs. <answer>) ensures sufficient training signal for both modes and prevents mode collapse. At inference, reasoning depth is then continuously tunable post-training by adjusting the decoding-probability threshold for triggering the <think> token, letting a single trained model trace out a range of points along an efficiency-performance Pareto frontier without any retraining or model modification.
one_liner: ADaPT diagnoses that existing efficiency-oriented RL methods fail because sequence-level efficiency rewards implicitly penalize correct-but-long reasoning (a structural mismatch, since only the first token -- the fast/slow mode choice -- actually determines efficiency, while all subsequent tokens can only affect correctness), and fixes this by applying an efficiency reward exclusively to a dedicated mode-selection <think>/<answer> token via a CISPO-stabilized token-level GRPO variant -- cutting Qwen2.5-7B's average generation length from 1540 to 1031 tokens (SFT+GRPO baseline) with only a 0.4-point accuracy drop, tracing a genuine Pareto frontier other methods stay strictly inside, and letting a single trained model's efficiency be tuned post-hoc by adjusting the mode-token's decoding threshold with no retraining.
problem: Large reasoning models apply long chain-of-thought uniformly regardless of query difficulty, wasting tokens on simple queries and sometimes harming accuracy through overthinking; existing efficiency-oriented methods (length-compression rewards, hybrid fast/slow routing) improve efficiency at the cost of reasoning performance because both scalarize efficiency and correctness into a single sequence-level training objective, which -- since a shorter answer among several correct candidates gets both correctness and efficiency reward while a longer-but-equally-correct answer gets only the correctness reward -- systematically disadvantages and suppresses correct long reasoning simply for being long, degrading deep reasoning capability whenever tasks genuinely require it.

relevance.overthinking: Directly and centrally relevant: it provides one of the clearest structural diagnoses in this archive of exactly why naive efficiency-oriented RL degrades reasoning -- proving via an MDP argument that only the first token controls efficiency, so applying an efficiency signal to every token misassigns credit to positions that cannot influence it -- and its fix (token-level reward decoupling plus a targeted clipping-stability correction for that specific token) is a more principled, mechanism-grounded version of the root-token/mode-gating idea also explored elsewhere in this archive (e.g. RPO), directly explaining, via its clipping-ratio measurements, why naive sequence-level or unweighted token-level RL rewards for length control tend to either collapse mode diversity or fail to learn a reliable gating policy at all.

results: Across Easy (CSQA, GSM8K, ARC) and Hard (MATH500, MMLU-Pro, Olympiad, AIME24) benchmark groups and two model scales (Qwen2.5-7B/3B-Base), ADaPT achieves the most favorable efficiency-performance balance among all compared methods: on Qwen2.5-7B, versus the strongest correctness-only baseline (SFT+GRPO), ADaPT reduces average generation length from 1540 to 1031 tokens (33% shorter) while accuracy drops only marginally (63.1%->62.7%); competing efficiency-oriented baselines (TLMRE, ARM, R-4B) reduce length by less while incurring more noticeable accuracy degradation, particularly on Hard tasks. A continuous Pareto-frontier analysis (varying the <think>-token decoding threshold post-training) shows ADaPT traces out a genuine frontier that dominates all compared baselines' accuracy-length trade-off points on both Easy and Hard task groups -- other methods' results fall strictly inside (below-and-to-the-right of) ADaPT's frontier, meaning at any matched token budget ADaPT achieves higher accuracy, and at any matched accuracy it uses fewer tokens. Mode-usage analysis (Easy/Hard task groups) shows ADaPT learns genuinely adaptive, task-sensitive mode selection: on Easy tasks it predominantly uses fast (<answer>) mode (71.3% ratio) achieving accuracy comparable to the always-slow-reasoning SFT+GRPO baseline (which relies on <think> 96.3% of the time) at far lower cost, while on Hard tasks it shifts substantially toward slow reasoning (79.3% <think> ratio, versus GRPO's 100%) while still preserving most of the accuracy -- direct evidence the token-level decoupled reward learns to use costly reasoning selectively rather than either indiscriminately (SFT+GRPO) or too sparingly (SFT alone, which mixes both modes with lower overall accuracy from lacking any mode-selection mechanism). Forcing ADaPT to always use slow reasoning (ADaPT_think, a constrained variant) matches or slightly exceeds SFT+GRPO's accuracy on most benchmarks (e.g. 63.7% vs. 63.1% average on Qwen2.5-7B), directly demonstrating that the token-level mode reward does not weaken the model's underlying deep-reasoning capability -- the capacity for complex multi-step reasoning is preserved intact, only its *invocation* becomes selective. Ablating the mode-reward tolerance parameter gamma shows a monotonic increase in <think>-mode usage as gamma rises from 0 to 1 for both 7B and 3B models, confirming gamma provides smooth, predictable control over reasoning depth; the smaller 3B model shows a stronger, earlier shift toward slow reasoning as gamma increases (surpassing the 7B model's <think> usage for gamma>=0.25), consistent with its lower fast-reasoning reliability and greater dependence on slow reasoning as a fallback. Clipping-ratio analysis directly validates the motivating diagnosis: under standard PPO/GRPO clipping, the empirical clip rate at the first (mode-selection) token is roughly two orders of magnitude higher than at all subsequent tokens throughout training, which the paper shows effectively nullifies the policy gradient at exactly the position that needs it most -- confirming the CISPO-based first-token-specific stabilization is necessary, not merely helpful, for reliable mode-selection learning.
